title: Declarative stream handler DSL and resilient example cookbook for Python SDK
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background:
We continue to receive support tickets and developer feedback around the Python SDK streaming chat surface: handlers are flexible but disparate, resume/checkpoint semantics are implemented ad-hoc by integrators, and examples primarily show low-level iterator plumbing. This leads to inconsistent retry/backpressure behavior across customers and repeated support work for resumability and graceful shutdown.

Goal:
Design and implement a declarative handler DSL (domain-specific surface) for the Python SDK that makes common patterns (checkpointing, idempotent emit, backpressure-aware processing, soft vs hard fail semantics, telemetry hooks, and graceful shutdown) easy to express. Ship a resilient example cookbook with production-ready recipes and migration guidelines.

Proposal summary:
- Introduce a small declarative decorator+context DSL: @stream_handler, with options for resume_key, commit_on_emit, max_uncommitted_events, and retry_policy.
- Provide two convenience base handler classes: ResumableSyncHandler and ResumableAsyncHandler, with careful type hints and minimal ceremony.
- Implement an internal checkpoint store abstraction with pluggable adapters (in-memory for tests, Redis, S3 checkpoints) and a default local file adapter for dev.
- Define explicit semantics for retries: soft-retry (idempotent emit only, can continue after transient errors) vs hard-retry (stop and bubble up after N attempts).
- Provide first-class telemetry hooks: on_event_received, on_commit, on_retry, on_backpressure. These invoke the SDK telemetry bridge used in our console.
- Ship a cookbook with 6 recipes (simple echo handler, user-message dedupe+checkpointing, batched inference with KV cache reuse, backpressure-aware external API calls, graceful shutdown with drain semantics, migration guide from existing callback patterns).

Design decisions and trade-offs:
- DSL vs explicit APIs: DSL reduces boilerplate and standardizes behavior for users. To avoid hiding complexity, all DSL knobs are also available on base handler classes.
- Checkpoint store default: we choose local file for dev/testing to avoid surprising network dependencies. Production adapters documented and implemented under python-sdk-checkpoints package.
- Retry semantics: default to conservative soft-retry with exponential backoff. Users can opt into stronger guarantees via retry_policy.

API sketch (illustrative):
from redwood.sdk.streaming import stream_handler, ResumableAsyncHandler, CheckpointStore, RetryPolicy

@stream_handler(resume_key_fn=lambda req: req.context.user_id, commit_on_emit=True, max_uncommitted_events=32)
class OrderHandler(ResumableAsyncHandler):
    async def handle_event(self, event):
        # idempotent processing guaranteed by SDK commit semantics
        output = await self._call_model(event.text)
        await self.emit(output)

handler = OrderHandler(checkpoint_store=CheckpointStore.local("/tmp/ckpts"))

Acceptance criteria (must be verifiable):
- The SDK exposes the new decorator and handler base classes in the python package with type hints and runtime validation.
- Checkpoint adapter interface implemented with in-memory (tests), local-file (dev), and Redis (integration) adapters.
- Cookbook contains 6 recipes listed above and at least 3 end-to-end examples (unit tests + integration test using Redis adapter).
- Retry semantics documented with example policies; default behavior runs in CI tests validating soft retry and hard retry flows.
- Telemetry hooks emit events to the SDK telemetry bridge; console shows sample traces for example workflow.
- Migration guide drafted and linked from SDK README.

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for handler lifecycle: event receive, emit, commit, resume after simulated crash, and graceful shutdown.
- Integration tests using ephemeral Redis in CI for checkpointing and resume validation across handler restarts.
- Performance microbench: measure added latency per message for the default handler path and ensure <1ms median overhead for a no-op handler.
- Fuzz tests to validate behavior under bursty event arrival and to ensure backpressure max_uncommitted_events prevents unbounded memory growth.

Rollout and docs:
- Beta feature behind feature flag in the SDK (feature_streaming_handler_v1).
- Publish docs: new section in streaming SDK docs, tutorial notebook, and migration guide.
- Announce to SDK users in weekly changelog and include code snippets in quickstart.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Developers rely on the DSL but need advanced control. Mitigation: Expose low-level APIs and document when to drop down.
- Risk: Checkpoint store correctness across adapters. Mitigation: Integration tests and a small formal spec in docs describing atomicity and visibility guarantees.
- Risk: Telemetry surface being noisy. Mitigation: sample rate config and opt-out option.

Open questions:
- Should the default checkpoint store use a namespaced path per org in local file adapter? (Proposal: yes, include user/org id).
- How do we ensure backwards compatibility with existing callback-based helpers? (Proposal: adaptor shim layer in the SDK that wraps old callbacks into the new handler).

Implementation milestones:
1) API design review + proto types and internal demo (2w)
2) Core handler and local-file checkpoint implementation + unit tests (1w)
3) Redis adapter + integration tests + CI job (1w)
4) Cookbook and migration guide + telemetry hooks wired (1w)
5) Performance testing, docs review, and beta release behind feature flag (1w)

Estimated effort: 8 points (~6 weeks with review/QA, see estimate above).
